speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to join with the working men and women of Canada, and indeed with all Canadians, in observing April 28 as the labour movement's national day of mourning to honour workers who are injured or killed on the job, or who suffer work-related diseases, and to draw greater attention to the serious and ever present problem of workplace safety and health.
The number of Canadian workers injured, killed, or made ill in the workplace every year constitutes a national tragedy.

The figures speak for themselves. In Canada every year, at least one out of every nine workers suffers a work-related injury. In 1986, the latest year for which full statistics are available, 869 Canadian workers were killed on the job, and 17.5 million person-days were lost due to accidents and injuries.
In addition to untold human suffering, these fatalities and injuries represent a loss of some 16 billion dollars in terms of direct and indirect costs-truly, a terrible burden for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, on this day I call on Hon. Members, on workers and employers and on all Canadians to stand together, resolved that we can and that we shall reduce this terrible toll, and that the price of our progress and our economic growth shall not be the lives and well-being of workers.
As Minister of Labour, this national day of mourning has special significance for me, since 1988 marks the 20th anniversary of the first federal occupational safety and health legislation in Canada.
Much progress has been made in this area over the past 20 years and today we see a growing trend to greater worker and employer involvement in occupational safety and health.
This ongoing trend recognizes that while laws and governmental organizations play an important role, in the final analysis it is the workers and employers who have the greatest role to play in preventing, eliminating or controlling hazards in the workplace.
Mr. Speaker, amendments made to the Canada Labour Code over the years have recognized and strengthened the right of workers to refuse dangerous work, the right of workers to be informed of hazards, and the right of workers and employers to participate in joint safety and health committees. All of these rights depend upon information. Information is the raw material from which are built co-operation and consensus.

The Government supports co-operation and consensusbuilding, and is always seeking new ways of giving workers and employers greater access to the information they need to prevent occupational injuries and illnesses.
An excellent example of this is the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System, known as WHMIS. This system, which will come into force nationally by October 31, 1988, is a joint effort of the federal, provincial, and territorial Governments and is the result of several years of consultation between Governments, industry, and organized labour.
The purpose of WHMIS is to establish a uniform identification system for dangerous ingredients in the workplace. It will ensure that the hazardous materials produced, imported, or used within workplaces in Canada are adequately identified by suppliers using standard criteria. It will also ensure that data sheets on hazardous materials are transmitted by suppliers to employers and, subsequently, to employees.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to report that the Government has recently allocated an additional $1.8 million for the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety in Hamilton. The Centre is a successful example of tripartite co-operation. It is responsible for providing Canadians with information about occupational health and safety which is trustworthy, comprehensive, and intelligible. Its electronic information management system will support WHMIS.
It has demonstrated that the information it supplies results in improvements in the workplace. Workers, managers, and professionals trust the information and use it. That trust is increased by the centre's workshops which bring them together to establish common ground.
We are taking other steps on the legislative front to improve occupational safety and health. On Tuesday last, Bill C-124,

April 28, 1988
Statements by Ministers
an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code, received second reading in the House. One of the purposes of this Bill is to provide better protection for certain Nova Scotia miners regulated by the Code. Because of the special risks involved in working in the Cape Breton coal mines, this Bill proposes, among other measures, to establish a tripartite coal mining safety commission.
Last year Hon. Members granted expeditious approval to a Bill which allows workers in the Flin Flon mineral area of northern Manitoba to be governed by a single, uniform, and modern set of regulations suited to the mining industry.
As another example of co-operation and consensus-building I would also mention the recent creation of the tripartite committee to look at one of the most dangerous occupations in Canada-the fishing industry. This committee, appointed by the federal and provincial Governments, is expected to make its recommendations this May.

As I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, the figures on occupational fatalities and injuries show that we indeed have cause to mourn. But there is also cause for optimism. For instance, in recent years-1985 and 1986-the rate of workers who suffer a work-related injury has been reduced from one in every eight workers to one in every nine workers.
Largely due to better informed employees and employers, this improvement is small, but encouraging. With the help of all concerned Canadians, Mr. Speaker, much has already been done and much more can and will be done to reduce the tragic toll of workplace accidents and illnesses.

After the statements of my colleagues, and with the permission of the House, I suggest that we observe one minute of silence out of respect for today.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to take this opportunity to join Canadian workers who today, on April 28, the labour movement's National Day of Mourning, honour the memory of those who were injured and also, unfortunately, those who were killed in the workplace.
Mr. Speaker, despite the legislation that, over the years, has been passed by this Parliament and by most provinces in Canada, the number of accidents and injuries in the workplace is still too high. I may remind the House that it was in 1968, under the Liberal Government, that the first federal legislation on occupational health and safety was passed.
Today, one worker out of nine is injured by accidents- fewer than in the past-but I say this is still too much. What
the statistics do not mention is the story behind the figures we read in the reports released by Statistics Canada.

The real story that statistics do not tell is that despite the fact that only one out of nine workers suffers injury today, a reduction from past figures, the one who suffers this injury must live not with the one out of nine statistics but with 100 per cent in his case. It is very hard on these people and their families.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to highlight the important role played by two well-known Quebecers in improving working conditions and occupational health and safety in the workplace.
First, I would like to mention the Hon. Jean Marchand, who represented the riding of Langelier in the House for many years and was appointed Minister. I think that if it had not been for his influence, the first occupational health and safety legislation passed by Parliament under a Liberal Government in 1968 might not have seen the light of day and been passed at all stages in the House.
Jean Marchand, who was very active in the Confederation of National Trade Unions, both as secretary and president, could not leave Parliament without leaving his mark in this way.
I would also like to mention the work done for many years by another very colourful member of the CNTU, Mr. Michel Chartrand, who was among the first in Quebec to warn about the hazards of the workplace which, at the time, were even more serious than they are today.
Those who have known the verve and eloquence of Michel Chartrand know what I mean, when I say that he defended very vigourously-and that is an understatement-and passionately the cause for better working conditions.
Mr. Speaker, the Party I represent, the Liberal Party of Canada, has always led the way in seeking improved health and safety conditions in the workplace. As I said earlier, it introduced the first piece of legislation in the House in this respect, and also worked with other governments over the years to improve working conditions. More recently, for instance, we helped to expedite legislation to provide for a Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System, the WHMIS. Just two days ago, we were rushing to adopt Bill C-124, whose purpose is to improve safety in coal mines and to create the Coal Mining Safety Commission, which will be responsible for approving equipment and methods used in coal mines.
Mr. Speaker, over the years, conditions in the workplace have changed for the better. There was a time when the workplace, especially construction sites and other industrial environments, was a place where danger lurked on all sides. Today, things have improved a great deal.
April 28, 1988

Nevertheless, we cannot afford to relax our efforts and so much remains to be done. In fact, the Minister said so earlier in his speech. One Canadian worker injured out of nine is better, but it is still unacceptable. This figure must be brought down, especially since it does not reflect the situation in industries where accidents are far more numerous, and to name just one, I would draw the attention of the House to the fact that among longshoremen in Canadian ports, which are under federal jurisdiction, the accident rate is much higher than the national average.
Finally, I invite Hon. Members from all Parties to join their efforts to improve conditions for Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party and myself to join with the Minister and with the spokesman for the Liberal Party in observing April 28 as the labour movement's national day of mourning to honour workers who are injured or killed on the job. May I say that, at some point, we in this Party hope that this will be more than just the labour movement's national day of mourning and that it will be a Canadian day of mourning for workers injured or killed on the job.
Our labour critic, the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) who is not able to be here today, introduced a Private Member's Bill to that effect on March 15, just one month ago. He introduced Bill C-286, an Act respecting a day of mourning for persons killed or injured in the workplace, which, if passed, would see April 28 designated as a day of mourning in remembrance of persons killed or injured in the workplace. We hope that this Bill may become the instrument by which April 28 will be set aside by all Canadians as a day of remembrance for those killed or injured in the workplace.
I might also say, because I do not think it has been raised to this point, that the origin of choosing April 28 as the labour movement's national day of mourning was done because April 28, 1914 when the first worker safety legislation was introduced in Ontario.
After the rather self-congratulatory comments of the Liberal spokesperson I cannot resist saying that it was some 53 years later, during which time we were governed mostly by Liberal Governments, before we saw the first occupational health and safety legislation at the federal level. It seems to be a sign of the struggle that working people have had over the years to get protective legislation, and it was not until 1968 that we had this kind of legislation at the federal level. Side by side with working people all those years has been the New Democratic Party; before that, the CCF; before that, the Independent Labour Party; and before that, all the predecessors of the movement we represent today. We are very proud to be able to speak today and to lend our voice to this observation.
Statements by Ministers
I come from a community whose oral history is scattered with names of people who have been killed on the job. I come from a railway community. I grew up in a community where so-and-so's grandfather or father was killed on the road or in the shop in such-and-such a year. We often think, when we think of injured workers or workers killed on the job, of the high rates of injury and death for miners, fishermen, and others. I do not in any way mean to diminish that by highlighting what is my own experience, but certainly that is the case with respect to railways and it continues to be.
Just in Winnipeg alone in the last few years a number of people have been killed. Engineer Don McMillan was killed when his unit left the track and went into the overpass at Symington. Last year a road crane fell over and knocked down a pole, which in turn fell on a young railroader killing him instantly. Just a couple of months ago a young woman, a switch person who was studying to be a surgeon, got her arm caught in a knuckle and lost her arm from the elbow down. Obviously she will no longer be able to be a surgeon, but hopefully she will still be able to pursue a successful medical career. These kinds of things are happening all the time, and I think it is only appropriate that we have a day on which we can call attention to them.
The Minister says that the number of Canadian workers injured or killed constitutes a national tragedy. Of course, no one would disagree with him. It is a national tragedy that much more could be done to prevent. We signal to the Minister that we intend to keep putting pressure on this Government, as we have on previous Governments, to keep making improvements.
We are glad to see some of the things that have been done recently-for instance, the institution of the Workplace Hazardous Information System, WMHIS as it is sometimes known for obvious reasons. We are glad to see that, but much more progress must be made. When we debated the Canada Health Act in the House in 1984, I recall that one amendment I moved which was accepted into the preamble of the Act was that health was related to occupational health and safety. That principle is now built into the most fundamental health legislation of our country, and that Government has a mandated right out of the Act itself to pursue that kind of an approach at every opportunity it gets.
The Minister says, "let us all stand together". No one can argue with that, but is standing together the kind of thing that we see in the Railway Safety Act where companies, for violations of safety, are fined $50,000, a drop in the bucket to them, whereas workers are hit with a $10,000 fine? A $10,000 fine is obviously much more significant to workers than a $50,000 fine for the CNR or the CPR, which is hardly more than a licence to break the rules.
As a result of the increasingly competitive economic atmosphere, which the Government is always so proud of trying to worsen through deregulation, free trade, et cetera, a lot of pressure is being put on workers to be what companies

April 28, 1988
Committee Reports
call "more efficient". Often what that efficiency means is taking safety short-cuts. They are often under pressure to take those short-cuts, but if something happens or is found out, then it is the employee who must take the consequences. This is a bind in which rail workers and others are constantly being put. It is a bind which the Minister and others did not try to address in the Railway Safety Act and which they have not addressed adequately. Until they address it, we will not be able to be part of this great "back-patting" exercise that happens on these kinds of days. We will have to say with all sincerity that much more remains to be done and that we do not intend to be silent until it is done.

CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE Mr. Jim Fulton (Skeena) moved:
That the fourth report of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs
and Northern Development, presented to the House on Wednesday, March 2,
1988, be concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased that this motion is before the House today. It is a matter of long-standing business that needs to be dealt with by Parliament, by the Minister and, I suppose, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney).
A brief history of what has happened to the Lubicon people is in order. Mr. Justice E. Davie Fulton, the former Minister of Justice of Canada, appeared before the Committee and the Committee took a majority vote to have Mr. Fulton attached as a mediator to the Lubicon matter, something which Mr. Fulton himself felt would be most appropriate. I think Hon. Members would agree that someone who is so widely respected by Canadians, having had a long and brilliant career in politics and as a Justice of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, would be a most appropriate person for this. I suppose it is fair to say that the former Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), took that view in that he appointed Mr. Fulton to prepare a report in relation to the Lubicon matter.
After having heard Mr. Fulton and after having heard representatives of the Lubicon including Chief Bernard Ominayak and his council and others, it was the Committee's firm view that Mr. Fulton could most appropriately act as a mediator in the matter between the Government of Canada, the Lubicon band, and obviously the Government of Alberta. We felt that the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs ought to be used as a conduit to try to achieve a satisfactory resolution to a long outstanding matter.
I think many Members of the House are unaware of the history and evolution of the sacred international treaties between the First Nations of Canada and various agencies of the Crown. In the case of some of the initial treaties in my Province of British Columbia, the Governor at the time, Governor Douglas, obtained and created treaties with 14 of the nations on Vancouver Island, and those are international treaties as has been recognized by the courts of British Columbia. Certainly the treaties from the Prairies, Treaty 6, Treaty 8 and others, particularly from Alberta, are also recognized internationally as sacred treaties which are legally binding on the Crown.
Just to give Hon. Members a brief synopsis of the history, back in 1899, because the band was not located on a main waterway, it was missed by the Treaty 8 party and scrip commissioners. They were travelling in that area of Alberta and northwestern British Columbia, preparing lists of aboriginal populations for the preparation of Treaty 8. For reasons of speed, I suppose, the Lubicon people were not included in the evaluations that were done in 1899 just prior to the signing of Treaty 8.
April 28, 1988

In 1939, the band was visited by officials of Indian Affairs who recognized them as as separate band and promised them a reserve. The band membership list was drawn up and was left open so that the names of members who were in the bush, at work, or elsewhere could be added at a later date.
In 1939 and 1940 land on the western end of Lubicon Lake was chosen as a reserve and was approved by both levels of Government-Alberta and Canada. In 1942 a member of the Department of Indian Affairs named McCrimmon decided to close the band membership list and to remove names of persons not registered by 1912, thereby taking retroactive action in removing names from the list after a third of a century. The incomplete Lubicon band list was then cut from 154 to 64 persons.
In 1943 and 1944 the report of Judge McKeen and a judicial inquiry under Judge McDonald came out in favour of the band regarding membership lists, but this was again shelved by the Department. In 1952, due to numerous oil company inquiries about the area, Alberta brought the question of the reserve to federal attention once more.
In 1952 and 1953 the local Indian agent determined that the Lubicon site was "too isolated and inconvenient", and met with the band to try to get them to agree to another site. Later in 1953 the Province gave the federal Government a 30-day ultimatum about the reserve, assuming that the reserve would be struck from the record if no reply was received. The federal Government did not reply.
Between 1952 and 1973, attempts were made to eliminate the band through transfer-illegitimate transfer, as I might point out-of band members to other bands and through enfranchisement.
In 1954 a mission school was built at Little Buffalo Lake and families gradually moved there to allow their children to attend school.
In 1970 an all-weather road was constructed by the provincial Government from Peace River to the Lubicon lands.
In 1973 the band's existence as as separate band was confirmed by Order in Council, and in 1975 the band tried to file a caveat to serve notice of their unextinguished aboriginal claim. The Province refused to accept the caveat and the hearing was postponed until a similar case in the Northwest Territories was concluded.
Of course, when that case was concluded in 1976, it came out against the native people but stated that had the law there been the same as in Alberta the result would have been the opposite, sending a very clear signal to both levels of Government to move and to move expeditiously to settle the outstanding claim, rights, and title of the Lubicon people.
A serious hitch came along in 1977. The provincial Government changed the law retroactively by passing Bill 29, and the Lubicon's case was then dismissed.
Motions
In 1980 many oil companies began operations in the area. These operations included the bulldozing of roads, the drilling of wells, and the building of pipelines. The band's selfsufficient traditional lifestyle was suddenly no longer possible. Moose had been the main source of meat, and the number of moose killed declined drastically from 120 in 1982 to 27 in 1983 and down to three in 1984.
We can see that the game were moving rapidly out of the area. As Mr. Justice E. Davie Fulton concluded in his report, the impact of the 400 gas and oil wells, the construction of the pipelines, and fires at the drill sites had razed over 600 square miles of territory traditionally used for hunting and trapping by the Lubicon people. That territory had been laid to waste.
I think Hon. Members should recall what Mr. Justice Peter Seaton had to say on the Meares Island case, a case that I think Members of the House should take the time to read. Mr. Justice Peter Seaton said that there are few if any imaginable aboriginal rights left after an area has been clear cut. I think the same understanding of the situation was related by Mr. Justice E. Davie Fulton in relation to this area that was burned and developed, an area historically used for not just thousands of years but for 10,000 or more years by the Lubicon-Cree.
In 1981 the community was declared a provincial hamlet and people were told to apply for leases to their land or to accept it as a gift. The Province then stated that the community could not be part of the land claim since it was now a provincial hamlet.
In 1982 the band applied for an injunction preventing further development, and the injunction was denied. The judge decided that the Indian way of life does not exist and that something that does not exist cannot be damaged.
In 1984 a fact-finding mission of the World Council of Churches substantiated the Lubicon's allegations of injustice. In that same year band members were told by the Province to remove unauthorized fences, corrals, and houses. They were told to apply for provincial leases or to purchase the land in order to keep their property there. The band responded by saying that they had never ceded their traditional lands and recognized no authority of the provincial Government over those lands. To apply for leases from the Province would recognize its authority and weaken their land claim.
In 1985 Mr. Justice E. Davie Fulton was appointed by the federal Government to study the situation, and his report is now well known, at least to those who have interest in this matter. In 1986 negotiations began but quickly broke down when it became apparent that promises to negotiate on the basis of the Fulton report were not being honoured and, in the same year, a boycott of the 1988 Calgary Winter Olympics was announced by the band to draw attention to their desperate situation and to denounce the actions of a provincial Government that would be receiving much attention and prestige from the event.

April 28, 1988
Motions
By 1987 the band was once again asked by the federal Government to negotiate on the basis of the Fulton report, as well as for the public release of the report and to have Fulton on as a mediator.
This issue has been given not just broad provincial coverage in Alberta by the media there and by newspapers, television, and radio nationally but also internationally. The plight of the Lubicon people and the mistreatment and maltreatment of them by both the Alberta Government and the federal Government have received notorious attention around the world. There are reasons for that.
The Minister responsible for Alberta Native Affairs, Milton Pahl, went so far as to tell the Alberta Legislature in 1984 that the Lubicon-Cree do not exist. He said: "They may have as few as nine members". Resistance by the Alberta and federal Governments to the band has been strong enough to attract attention from the international human rights community. The director of the program to combat racism of the World Council of Churches in Geneva studied the case in 1983 and concluded that in the last couple of years the Alberta provincial Government and dozens of multinational oil companies have taken actions that could have genocidal consequences.
The United Nations Human Rights Committee studied the case for three years and concluded last summer that the rights of the Lubicon-Cree were being seriously abused. A full hearing of the case is to be held later this year in Geneva.
While E. Davie Fulton was studying the matter for the Government of Canada and the Lubicon people, he had a number of things to say. He was interviewed by John Goddard in an excellent article published in Saturday Night magazine in February of this year. In relation to the exploratory and development work done on the lands of the Lubicon, the article indicates:
Fulton expressed surprise at the extent of the work. Nearly 400 oil wells had been drilled within a ten-mile radius of Little Buffalo. Fulton also expressed surprise at the fire damage: 641 square miles of bush destroyed in the first three years of the oil boom... "I have seen the terrible effects of development"...
"I want to try to do something about it." ... I now realize that there are an appreciable number of Indians in Canada proper whose situations have never been settled"... "This particular band, God help them, was promised a settlement in 1940, and they're still waiting for it forty-seven years later. Their situation cries out for just and equitable treatment".
That is what the former Minister of Justice under John Diefenbaker and a former Justice of the Supreme Court had to say. The article continues:
The Member for Peace River, Jack Sissons (later the famous flying judge of the far north), declared himself "incensed," and summarized numerous complaints for the Minister: "that striking these persons off the lists was arbitrary, discreditable and indefensible; that these were Hitler tactics; that the Government has broken faith with the Indians; that the action indicates that there is in the Department lack of proper knowledge of the Indians and the territory; that the Indians are being treated like dogs; that this is oppression of the weak by the strong; that these people have no one to fight for them; that the Department is indifferent and unsympathetic to the welfare of
the Indians; and generally that the action is contrary to both the spirit and the letter of the Indian Act."
That is pretty strong language, but I think it hits the nail on the head. Mr. Fulton, who the Committee has proposed to act as a mediator, has accepted in principle the need for someone of his experience and understanding of the matter. He is now 71 years of age. He was the federal Justice Minister and Attorney General of Canada from 1957 to 1962 and a B.C. Supreme Court Judge from 1973 to 1981. As Don Braid pointed out in an article written earlier this year:
There's only one move that will work. Bill McKnight should call and ask him to mediate the claim.
The number's in the book, under LAWYERS. Fulton answers his phone very quickly these days.
A matter which occurred earlier this year also deserves the attention of all Members of this House. The Committee is disturbed and concerned about it. I know that my friend, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), will have much to say about the problems which have been created by the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) by his lack of attention to how this situation has caused such great concern in Canada and internationally.
As was pointed out by the national Chief of the Assembly of First Nations in an article in the Calgary Herald under the headline "McKnight in conflict of interest: native leader":
Indian Affairs Minister Bill McKnight has bungled the Lubicon land claim and his entire portfolio and must be replaced, says the national chief of the Assembly of First Nations.
Erasmus said McKnight is in conflict of interest, responsible for Indians as well as Minister in charge of the western diversification fund, which has given $9.5 million to a Japanese pulp company given timber rights on the Lubicon's traditional territory.
Erasmus blasted the federal Government's offer last week of $500,000 compensation to the Lubicons for lost treaty benefits.
"He offers half a million dollars for lost treaty benefits to the Crees of Lubicon, who never signed a treaty, then he hands a foreign company 19 times that much, $9.5 million, plus the timber resources of the Lubicons ... it's an outrage."
We know that the Government of Alberta has agreed, without ever tendering so that Canadian companies could bid on the lands or others could be involved in a democratically appropriate process, to transfer 11,000 square miles to Daishowa pulp company earlier this year. The conflict of interest was very clear and I confirmed it with departmental officials. A cabinet order required the Minister of Indian Affairs, in his responsibilities for both that and the Western Diversification office, to conduct an initial environmental impact evaluation of the proposal to build a pulp mill on the Peace River, both in terms of its impact on the Lubicon people and also in terms of its impact on federal matters, aboriginal matters, and aboriginal lands, particularly those that lie in the Lubicon traditional territory and in Wood Buffalo National Park. That was never done.
Therefore, the Minister is clearly in a conflict of interest for providing money to the Daishowa pulp project without having
April 28, 1988

complied with a cabinet order. He also has not stood up for the sacred trust responsibility he has to the Lubicon people by allowing the very lands which were under negotiation to be transferred untendered, lock, stock, and barrel, to a foreign-owned corporation.
In February the all-Party House of Commons Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs, of which I am a member, urged the appointment of Conservative Justice Minister Davie Fulton to reach a settlement in the band dispute. An article in The Globe and Mail of February 10, 1988, by Graham Fraser reads:
The former British Columbia Supreme Court justice said yesterday that he is prepared at any time to take part in the negotiations.
"I'm anxious to do anything I can to bring about a just and equitable solution," he told The Aboriginal and Northern Affairs Committee.
Mr. Fulton said he feels that within three to six months, it should be possible to see if there is a basis for agreement.
Today we could well have been on the verge of a satisfactory settlement for the Lubicon people, if the Minister had seen fit to put a very knowledgeable and respected Canadian at the helm of a process which he and the Governments of Canada and Alberta have bungled so badly for so many years.
The article goes on to say:
However, he also told the committee that Indian and Northern Affairs Minister William McKnight is opposed to his involvement in the issue.
"He has stated that he feels that I have stated an opinion that is unacceptable to the Government of Canada, and that on that basis, I would be a prejudiced party," Mr. Fulton said. "His opinion is based on a misreading of my report."
In relation to the impact of recent years of development he said:
As a result ... it became impossible for the Lubicon to continue hunting and trapping on the land.
In 1940, the federal Government agreed to grant the band about 50 hectares per individual, based on a population of 127, which would have amounted to about 65 square kilometers.
The Alberta Government has agreed to this amount, but no more, and has said it will challenge any figure above that.
The proposed pulp mill is an irritant which must be overcome. The Government of Canada must take its responsibility much more seriously. There are no signs of that from the present Minister and I think it is now up to the Prime Minister to take the bull by the horns and either replace the Minister or accept the recommendation which was put forward in good faith by all members of the Standing Committee.
This is not only an NDP idea or a Liberal idea or a Conservative idea. Members from all three Parties made a very serious recommendation, after having heard evidence which the Minister never heard, after after having heard E. Davie Fulton, after having studied the issue and heard the views of Albertans, and having heard recommendations of sources from around the country including the First Nations of Canada and others.
Motions
We should listen, from time to time, to pressure from people such as Archbishop Ted Scott, the President of the Canadian Council of Churches, who telexed the Prime Minister following the decision made by the Standing Committee on this matter. On behalf of the Canadian Council of Churches, Archbishop Scott urged the Prime Minister "to immediately implement the resolution passed today by the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development calling on the Government of Canada to initiate bilateral negotiations with the Lubicon Lake Indian band over the next six months and to appoint the Hon. E. Davie Fulton as mediator in a determined effort to seek a just settlement on this long, outstanding land claims dispute". That is from the February 9 telex message from Ted Scott to the Prime Minister.
There are groups in Canada and groups around the world that take this issue very seriously. The Standing Committee has an opportunity, two months after we made this recommendation, to reflect on the fact that there has been very little progress in these many months since we tried to stimulate at least the process that had some hope of success. Rather than that, we have seen the Government of Alberta and the Government of Canada continue, both here in Canada and at the international level, to try to block the legitimate aspirations of the Lubicon people for a fair settlement.
As First Nations and as original inhabitants and occupants of Canada, I think it is high time this Parliament listened carefully and involved someone such as E. Davie Fulton as a mediator to find a just settlement.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member talked about the reduction of the population of the Lubicon band in 1944 from 164 to 127 persons. What was the basis for this reduction? What was the effect of that as far as the band and its claims were concerned?

Mr. Speaker, that question is key to the kind of jiggery-pokery that has gone on for a long time, both at the bureaucratic and political level.
In 1942 a man named McCrimmon, a paid bureaucratic with the Department of Indian Affairs, decided to close the band membership list and remove the names of persons not registered by 1912. A bureaucrat unilaterally decided that 30 years of history would be suddenly undone and that all of those individuals who had been added during that 30-year period would simply be wiped off the list. That cut the Lubicon Lake band list from 154 to 64 persons.
We can see that that kind of thought process has continued throughout this century. I quoted Milton Pahl speaking in the Alberta Legislature, who claimed just three years ago that there were only nine Lubicons and that the Lubicon band did not exist.

April 28, 1988
Motions
The fact is that the Lubicons, who had an extensive genealogical survey done, have continued to point out that at least as of November last year there were 457 Lubicon people. That is the basis of the dispute being put forward by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in the House. He claims that that may not be the right number. The Government of Alberta would like to claim that there are no Lubicons, but national and international opinion has turned against that kind of blindness to reality.
Over 500 bands in this country face a continuing problem in having Canadians, particularly elected Governments, understand the basis of their claim that they were original occupants of North America when the French and English arrived. Even at the time when Columbus was lost at sea this hemisphere was very heavily occupied.
Historians now believe that at the time of contact there were as many as 400,000 aboriginal occupants on the coast of the Pacific northwest. Let us recognize the treaties as being the sacred international documents they are. This is something against which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has been fighting in Geneva.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) and others have been fighting against this at the ILO. We have to understand that these are sovereign people who were the original occupants of this continent.
The Supreme Court of Canada, the highest court in this land, recognized unanimously in 1972 that aboriginal title exists and is outstanding in Canada. How Parliaments and Legislatures go about settling that is something the court has backed away from for many years. In fact, there was a three-three tie on the famed Calder case. Rather than making a decision, it wanted legislatures to negotiate and arrive at fair settlements. That is something that neither Premier Getty nor the Prime Minister are prepared to do at this point for the Lubicons and other outstanding specific and comprehensive claims.
The numbers game that was illegitimately played in 1942 by Mr. McCrimmon has been attempted again by Milton Pahl in the Alberta Legislature and by the Prime Minister. I think it is high time that we recognize the rights of the Lubicon people to determine their membership and get on with the important job of finding a mediator, such as Mr. Fulton, who can bring about a fair and just settlement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
There you see it again, Mr. Speaker. When we are trying to debate this Bill, we get interruptions. I wish the members of the NDP would become serious about this and would let us pass this legislation.
As I was saying, this is an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of western Canada. This Government came to power committed to a new approach to regional development. Bill C-113, similar legislation for the Atlantic region and regional initiatives in Ontario and Quebec demonstrate that this Government is making the effort to change long established institutional practices in a way that more accurately reflects the regional realities of Canada.
I was pleased to see that the legislative committee and Members of the House have been able to deal with this Bill so quickly. We hope that we have speedy approval here today.
I find that there is widespread support for the western diversification initiative, but there is a certain impatience because we do not already have in place this important legislative tool to do the job that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) set out for us last August when he announced the initiative.
In designing the western diversification initiative and the present legislation, westerners in the business community, labour, and Government expressed their concerns and gave their ideas on what they would like to see the federal Government do to encourage development in the West. This initiative has benefitted from their contributions.
In Government, I would particularly like to draw attention to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) and to my other western colleagues for the work they have done in bringing forward this initiative.
Now that Hon. Members have had time to review the legislation, they will see that the work was well worth the effort. A piece of enabling legislation has been put forward that provides a solid foundation for building an effective Department specifically designed to meet the needs and conditions of the West.
Natural resources are the West's major economic strength and its major economic weakness. Our reliance on producing a few commodities leaves us exposed to downturns in the economy that result in depressed sales and prices. If there is one thing on which westerners are agreed, it is on the need to even out the economic roller-coaster through diversification of the economy.
Diversification is not something that can be commanded or directed from Ottawa. It must come from the people in the West with ideas, talent, and commitment. Only they can seize the opportunities available.
We know from discussions with westerners and from the nearly 3,000 proposals, the 4,000 office visits, and the 50,000 telephone inquiries received by western diversification that the ideas are there as are the people who can put them into action.
This Government has done much to create the right climate for economic growth and investment and to reinvigorate the West. In coming to the aid of western farmers, removing
April 28, 1988

unjust energy policies and taxes, and helping the transportation sector, we have released new vitality and economic renewal. The western diversification initiative is now encouraging, directly and indirectly, the people and the enterprises with the good ideas to diversify the economy and thus make it less vulnerable.
The purpose of Bill C-113 is to promote development and diversification in the West and to advance the interests of the West in federal decision-making. In other words, westerners will now have a Department to which they can turn for assistance and which speaks for their interests in government.
In the West we know that the distance from Ottawa to Saskatoon is much greater than the distance from Saskatoon to Ottawa. The new Department and the Deputy Minister are to be based in Edmonton. Regional offices with Assistant Deputy Ministers in charge are to be located in Vancouver, Saskatoon, and Winnipeg. Westerners will have easy access to the Department and senior officials will be more in tune with the concerns and problems of the West. The office will promote a regionally based, not Ottawa imposed, approach to economic development.
Pathfinding is an important function of these offices. Small businesses often cannot afford the time or expense to look for government assistance. To date, more than 70 firms have been assisted in finding appropriate government support outside that offered by western diversification.
The Ottawa liaison office will perform the advocacy role. The Bill gives the Minister authority to guide and lead in the creation of government policies and programs for the West. As well, the Minister and the Department have the power to formulate plans and integrated strategies and, where appropriate, to oversee them.
We heard in the Commons debate during second reading that the Ottawa office lacked the capability to perform its important advocacy role. The Opposition seemed to be suggesting that the Department should be Ottawa based. I want to assure Hon. Members that we do not share that view. The Ottawa office will, however, be staffed in numbers and in rank sufficient to do the job. Already the office is having an impact, and its influence will grow in shaping national policies and national expenditures from a western point of view.
The use of these advocacy powers at the centre of government will ensure that government actions are sensitive to western concerns and issues. Furthermore, the Department will work to overcome piecemeal approaches to development and diversification.
The Government recognizes that small and medium-sized enterprises offer great potential for achieving economic diversification. Statistics Canada tells us that firms with fewer than 20 employees were responsible for 80 per cent of all net job creation in the West in the years 1978 to 1984. Seventy-five per cent of these new jobs came from firms that did not exist before 1978. We know from western diversification's own
Western Economic Diversification Act
records that small business is interested in the type of support western diversification offers.
Western diversification is responsive to small business. Many of the projects approved for support have been awarded to small businesses. Roughly 70 per cent of approvals have been for funds less than $100,000. This assistance has been given under existing authorities. With passage of the legislation, the Department will give special attention to how to further encourage these types of enterprises.
The legislation is not restrictive. If WD can achieve its objectives by working with larger enterprises, the Department has the authority to act. WD is particularly interested in supporting endeavours that will have widespread systemic effects that ripple through an economic sector to benefit both small and large enterprises.
One of the main thrusts of the western diversification initiative is the Western Diversification Fund. The legislation authorizes ways in which the Department can offer financial assistance for proposals that further diversification.
The legislative committee heard that small business in the West is not looking for government hand-outs. They expressed a particular desire for federal government support to make up for the inadequacies of existing financial institutions that fail to meet the financing needs.
The legislation before us today gives the Department of Western Economic Diversification the power to offer loans, loan guarantees, and credit insurance. The Department will be in a better position to complement existing financial institutions and services by being able to offer a wide range of financial assistance once this Bill is passed.
Again we heard of the desire for federal support for small business development corporations and other innovative arrangements to respond to local initiatives. The present legislation gives WD the authority and the flexibility to participate in any such arrangements that will improve the business environment in the West and lead to economic diversification.
Flexibility and innovation will be the keys to success. We know that the problems of the West cannot be solved by simply throwing money at them. However, financial assistance can be effective if used strategically to help implement initiatives that create new opportunities for an economic sector or open up new areas of economic activity.
To date western diversification has been restricted in the financial assistance it can offer. With passage of the legislation the Department will have more options to tailor financial assistance better to the needs of people and business with good ideas.
In broad terms western diversification wants to encourage investments in areas that promote new technologies, develop

April 28, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
new markets, replace products that the West imports, make use of under-utilized resources, and increase productivity.
The legislation before us is innovative and long overdue. The problems of the West are real, and we have an obligation to see that the institutions and policies are put in place to deal with them. This legislation enables us to get on with the job.
The new Department created by this legislation will give the West a strong voice in contributing to national decisionmaking, in influencing the machinery of government to respond more effectively and equitably to western needs, and in gaining greater access to national economic programs.
The Department will administer its programs and the Western Diversification Fund in a manner designed to broaden the economic base of the West. The Department, in summary, has the co-ordinating role of a central agency and the operating role of a line Department.
The legislation provides a firm foundation for an innovative new approach to regional development and for tackling the problems holding back diversification of the western economy. The quicker we can get on with the job the better. I urge speedy approval of Bill C-113. Therefore I move:
That the House continue to sit through the lunch hour for the purpose of continuing consideration of Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of Western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts.

Therefore, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) has the floor on debate.

Mr. Speaker, every Member of the House, particularly those from western Canada, supports western diversification. The issue in this debate is whether this is the most effective, most useful, and most productive way of achieving it. Unfortunately the Government has tried to pretend that western diversification only starts with the passage of this Bill. Unfortunately it ignores the other initiatives and programs which have been applied to western Canada. It has made no attempt to learn from those programs what the basic federal responsibility and requirements should be.
Part of the reason for that has been the haste. An almost frantic anxiety over this Bill was most clearly demonstrated when the Bill was given second reading, after very moderate debate, and Conservative members of the committee undertook to embargo any kind of committee work whatsoever. There were no representations, no witnesses, and no examination. They tried to railroad the Bill right through Parliament. It was only after we appealed to the Chair that we be given our minimal parliamentary rights that we were able to rescind the incredible Draconian suppression of parliamentary prerogatives and rights. Even then we were allowed the sum total of three and four witnesses, even though there was a much more extensive list of people who wanted to attend.
Putting into place legislation as important as this one would have assumed that there should have been broad and extensive consultation. There was much greater anxiety to have an election goodie on the Government's list of achievements than to have good legislation. There was no effort to think carefully through what was being done. There are some very serious flaws in the legislation which will handicap the efforts of future Governments to apply the resources and initiatives required in western Canada.
One reason for that is that there is once again a major difference in philosophy. The Government in power believes that the only way to develop a country or region is through individual activities and individual enterprises. It sees no constructive, positive, creative roles for the public sector working in partnership with private business. There is a blindfold on what has been the genius of Canadian history, that is, the development of this country through a mixed economy, a combined effort of various public and private sector initiatives.
It has often been the public sector which has had to make the major, strategic choice and has tried to put out a blueprint. It has not simply left it up to the market-place to determine what will be developed and how and where it will be developed. That is of particular importance in a region like western Canada where there is not a large private sector. We do not have big corporations and vast networks of businesses such as exist in southern Ontario. That is why public sector involvement has been very crucial, yet all we have seen since the Government came to power in 1984 is the dismemberment of many important development initiatives by the public sector in western Canada.
April 28, 1988

Let us use the example of Petro-Canada, a Crown corporation. The previous Government had established a research centre called Canertech, which was to provide special funding and initiatives in the area of renewable resources. It was to find an alternative, such as ethynol or hydrogen power, so that we could get away from the idea that our energy is based solely upon non-renewable resources. That institute was cancelled even though it had established a very good working relationship with a number of businesses and research institutions. Petro-Canada wiped out the jobs of 280 research workers in its own organization.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) says that what we really require in Canada is more research and development. He says that we need more scientists, engineers, and others working in practical areas of research. Yet, his own Crown corporation closes down its research facilities in the City of Calgary, throwing 280 people out on the streets.
How can the Government talk about research and development when it is retreating from that important field? Must we rely on a small business with a cash flow of perhaps $4 million or $5 million to duplicate what Petro-Canada did? Of course it cannot be done. Research is not taking place because the Government does not recognize the effectiveness of having public sector initiated research and development. It has a blind ideological obsession that the private sector is good and the public sector is bad. It is a kind of Manichaean dichotomy about what is good and what is bad in the world.
There must be a proper balance between the two in western Canada. The western diversification fund does not provide the kind of blueprint by which western Canada will be able to enter an economy that is increasingly dominated by high technology and information sciences. Most small and medium sized businesses do not have the capacity to mount the kind of research and development that goes into these areas.
I want to refer to an interesting document entitled "Innovation Policy in the Western Provinces". It was put out by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, perhaps one of the best known and most highly regarded economic research institutions in the world. It deals with the economic requirements of the major industrial states.
What are the primary recommendations in this document? One is that there must be a number of public sector infrastructure investments at both the provincial and federal level in order to ensure that the western Canadian economy in the four western provinces acquires the capacity to mobilize resources to compete in a high-tech age. Yet the western diversification legislation excludes investment infrastructure, the very thing the organization says that we need. It cannot be done with this Bill.
Since 1970 the federal Government of the day invested in over 30 research centres in western Canada. These were situated at universities or independent organizations in a
Western Economic Diversification Act
deliberate attempt to counterbalance the concentration of scientific activity in central Canada and to make sure western Canada had adequate opportunities in such areas as microelectronics, biotechnology, and industrial research. Many of those were closed down by the Government, or the funding was restricted.
At one time the National Research Council had over 5,000 personnel in western Canada. That number has decreased as a result of cut-backs.
The advocates of this legislation say that they are trying to encourage the diversification of the western economy, but the fact is they have been the culprits in cutting back and removing the kind of investment that would be required to bring about that development. This legislation does not address that issue.
Let me also point out what I believe is a fraudulent statement on the part of the Parliamentary Secretary who introduced third reading, as well as other Members. They suggested that this will represent the opening round of opportunities for western businesses to get loans and grants in order to expand their businesses or work in new areas. That is a falsehood.
Is the Parliamentary Secretary totally unaware of the Economic Regional Development Agreements that have been working in the western provinces since 1980? They will contribute more money in those four years than is contained in the western diversification fund. The total investment from ERDA was $2.1 billion as opposed to the $1.2 billion in this western diversification fund.
We asked the Minister in committee whether the ERDA will continue. He said that they have not yet made up their minds. In other words, he is saying that this is replacing the ERDA programs.

April 28, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act

Mr. Speaker, we just saw a graphic example of the level of interest in this debate shown by western members of the Conservative Party. They were so concerned about the parliamentary process that they had to hide behind the curtains in order to engage in a proper dialogue.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The Hon. Member has been here for a very long time. He knows that equipment in the House has changed and there are televisions outside the Chamber on which Members can watch the debate.
I appreciate that there must be a quorum in the House, but I would not want the Hon. Member to reflect on whether Members are inside or outside the House. He knows that, and I do not have to bring it to his attention.

Mr. Speaker, I was only concerned that most Tory Members have not learned how to turn on a TV yet. Now that you have assured me that they have reached that level, I will continue with my remarks.
We were talking about the Economic Regional Development Agreements which have provided twice the amount of funding in the first four years than is available under this Bill. It is significant to note that the Minister was not prepared to make a commitment that that program will continue.
If one draws the logical conclusion, the western diversification fund will provide half the funding that ERDA programs did. In other words, we have a 50 per cent cut-back on our hands. There is no assurance or guarantee that there will be any form of replacement for those funds, to say nothing of the fact the Government is cancelling the Industrial Research and Development Program, IRDP, plus many other programs under DRIE. What we really have here is a placebo. It is once again an attempt to gussy up, to put on the cosmetics, but to take away the substance and retract the kinds of investments that are required.
There are some very serious questions about the ability or willingness under this particular Bill of the Government to establish priorities. When questions were asked about whether there would be commitments on major funding of irrigation and water projects, for instance, which are absolutely essential to rescue the incredible erosion happening on prairie lands and very crucial to the continuation of our food industry, there was absolutely no commitment or willingness to say it was possible as part of western diversification. There is no sense that the federal Government has anything more than a kind of handout role to play.
At this crucial stage I think we must pioneer various ways of co-ordinating and co-operating, not just having more federal-provincial meetings, which is the only industry this Government seems to be able to generate, but actually pooling capital and putting our combined resources together to make major investments in highways, research centres, and irrigation projects.
I think it is fair to say that one of the most important kinds of investments the Government can make in terms of diversifying an economy is to ensure there is an attractive environment in which private sector investment will be made. The OECD study confirms that. We must have a village, town or city with good water, good roads, and good schools. That is where the public sector comes into play. The municipalities of western Canada, together with their confreres in other parts of Canada, have said that the most serious drawback to development is the deterioration of the infrastructure of our villages, towns, and cities.
When we specifically asked about this program, we were told that that kind of investment was also excluded, was not possible. The point I am making is that when it comes to good economic development strategy, this Bill does not provide us with the tools. All it does is continue a basic grant program which was available under other programs. That is it.
We are told that somehow there would be regional offices and more access. We can argue that there were regional offices before and Federal Economic Development Co-ordinators. DRIE had an office in every province. The applications were there. There is absolutely no difference whatsoever in concept or in execution. The Government is just giving it a new name. It is just changing the sign board, that is all.
The fact is that the Government is cutting back the money, excluding various forms of investment, refusing to provide leadership, but is changing the name. That is the sum total of the Western Diversification Program in front of us. More than that, there is something I think is a tell-tale sign of the future. For the first time a Government of Canada is now taking applications for support from the federal Government in regional development and submitting it to a test. What is that test? Does it meet the requirements of the U.S. trade law? If the Government considers in its judgment that somehow a business applying for help under western diversification may run counter to U.S. trade law, it will not receive any money. Everything must be censored through the Department of External Affairs.
In spite of all the assertions made by the Prime Minister, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), and the rest of that crowd over there that regional development will not be affected by the free trade deal, we have clear evidence that that in fact is not true. They admit they are now taking regional development programs and submitting them to a criteria based upon U.S. trade law. If they think it will be countervailable or a consequence of anti-dumping, they will not approve it. That is a forecast for the future.
In fact, all our regional development programs will now be subject to an advanced censorship by the federal Government in terms of its impact upon U.S. trade law. When we consider that U.S. trade law is getting tougher day by day, such as redefining the notion of a subsidy, we see that our regional development programs will be substantially affected and restricted as a consequence of the proposed trade agreement.
April 28, 1988

In this Bill we have proof positive that the guarantees and the assurances of the Prime Minister are absolutely worth nothing. They are as good as his commitment on acid rain and indexing senior citizens' pensions, and all those sacred trusts he used to like to talk about. We have just seen another sacred trust broken with this Bill.
While we approve the principle and the necessity to develop a western economy, I suggest that this is a faulty way of doing it. It will result in less resources being allocated. It appears that it will not provide the kinds of significant federal investments in the West which are desperately needed. More important, it bootlegs a severe restriction on regional development practices because of its adherence to U.S. trade laws being the basis for judgment as to whether or not one receive a grant. I suggest that that is a pretty severe and negative condemnation of this piece of legislation.
All I can say is that if the House passes the Bill and it goes to the second Chamber and is passed there, it will be up to another Government to change the policy substantially and substantially reorganize western diversification to take away the restrictions, the exemptions, and once again put the federal Government in a place where it can provide real leadership, partnership, and real investment to western Canada so that that region can meet the challenges of a new age based on high technology. That is where we have to go. This Bill will not take us there.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on the western diversification Bill. This morning the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) tried to bring before this House the problems of the Lubicon Indian band land claims. The Hon. Member was frustrated in that endeavour by an action taken by the Government to bring before the House this particular Bill to establish the department of western economic diversification. That kind of action, taken on behalf of the Government by the Minister who moved the motion, is typical of the attitude of the Government toward the Indian people and toward the promises it made to the Indian people and to all citizens of Canada. It is contrary to the trust the Government accepted when it became the Government on September 4, 1984.
Since 1940 and earlier the Lubicon Indians have been attempting to establish their rights with succeeding Governments and to put before the Government and the people of Canada the unfair treatment they received over a long period of time. They called upon succeeding Governments to do something about fulfilling those rights. They did not sign a treaty in the original treaty signatures, and they did not cede their land. Therefore, in the eyes of most people, they still own that land and as a sovereign nation they should be dealt with in that fashion.
Western Economic Diversification Act
I dwell on that issue in	the	debate on this	particular Billbecause that trust	will be	an	important part	of success orfailure in this particular Bill; trust, not only with the Indian people, but because of the economy of the Indian nations across the West that is of major importance in western development and western diversification. If we allow the condition of native	people	in western Canada	to deteriorateany further, or if	we do	not	take action on	objectionable
situations already in place such as that of the Lubicon people, then we will be faced with the condemnation of the world and will be unable to take meaningful action to improve the economies of native communities in the West.
What happened this morning is that the Government cut off its nose to spite its face by not allowing the House to move forward on the Lubicon affair and to solve it and, in the process of solving it, establish a structure by which land claims can be made to have a major impact upon diversification and development of Indian nations in the West. Unless we put our house in order in the West, the impact of legislation such as this will be minimal.
The principles of the Department we are talking about today and the principles of this Bill are supported by all Members of the House and the people of western Canada. It is not the matter of the principle of the Bill we are discussing today. It is the matter of whether or not the Bill will be successful after it is put in place. The offices have been in place for a considerable length of time. To judge from action or what has happened until now we cannot be too sure that there will be a great deal of success. There has been a lot of interest on the part of the people, developed by the propaganda put forward by the Government in establishing this Bill when it was announced in Edmonton. It has been announced on several occasions successively, as well as the discussion we have had in the House on it.
This Bill states that there will be an office that will attempt to diversify the economy of western Canada. That is something that has been needed for many years in western Canada and in other parts of Canada. It is also something that we have had for many years in some form or another. Therefore, attempts to diversify have been attempted many times for many years in many parts of Canada. Why have they not worked? If we looked at the reasons that they have not worked, we might find a good structure and a good basis under which to be sure that the western diversification offices will have some long-term impact. That is a key requirement, as far as economic development is concerned.
The Government seems to be putting a considerable amount of hope and a great deal of store in having a head office in Edmonton and a branch in Saskatoon. That in itself is bound to create a little economic diversification and jobs, but it is not the aim of the Bill or of the Department as it develops.
Under the present circumstances, or from the history that we have of past actions by government diversification projects,

April 28, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
it is not a guarantee of success or even of action. An application filed, looked at, returned, discussed, and filed again is not action. To a great extent that seems to be what has been going on.
What has happened in the past is that companies that develop in marginal situations where either the population does not establish the type of markets which they must fulfil, or the transportation costs are so high that they become a factor in success of a particular industry, those operations of initial actions may at first appear to be successful. We have the history of meat packing in Prince Edward Island and the history of industries which have developed and have seemingly been a success. While the Government puts in place the assistance that will keep that operation going for a little while, it stays operating. When the cream of government assistance has been skimmed off and it comes down to the nitty-gritty of dealing with the market, the support is not there and then the industry packs up and leaves. That is the historical situation that we have faced in many parts of the country, many times, in attempting to establish some type of diversification in areas.
I commenced by stating that there was a need to establish some type of trust as far as the Government was concerned. The Government can do that by dealing with the land claims of native communities.
The Government could also deal with that with the provinces by fulfilling promises that it made. Before and after the Government was elected, on many occasions it promised that it would help to diversify the economies or to improve the economies of both the East and the West by increasing the amount of government procurement that actually took place in the Atlantic provinces or in the West. How has the Government fulfilled that promise? In 1984-85, the first year of being in office, the percentage of procurement for the western provinces, that is purchases within those provinces by the Government of Canada, was 13.4 per cent. After many promises and much pushing by the Government to increase it and make it more even across the country, it went from 13.9 per cent in 1984-85 to 12.8 per cent in 1985-86.
We must remember that a premise of the national Government is to increase the amount of purchases in the West. In 1986-87 we went down further still. In 1986-87 the purchases of government through the Department of Supply and Services in western Canada went down to 11.5 per cent of the total. In other words, we do not have any good indication that the Government will do the things that it promises to do, if we look at purchases by Supply and Services as an indication of how it will fulfil those promises.
There are a number of other points that should be brought up in discussing the possibility of the success of the Western Diversification Department. There has been a tendency on the part of the Government to say: "Once you get it out there, because it is out there, it will work". The Liberals said that on
many occasions before, as far as western Canada was concerned.
What does this Bill do and what does it not do? First, it does not do a very good job of defining what diversification is. If there is to be real diversification in western Canada, then it would seem that we must know where we will find the type of diversification and what it should be. The Government seems to be taking initiatives through this action, through this office, and through this Bill is to emphasize the building on existing resource structures that are already in place. That probably sounds like a good and easy way to move. It even sounds very logical. It also has been the basis of many western attempts at diversification in the past. It has not worked.
When one bought a bag of flour in the West, as you know, Mr. Speaker, some 30 years ago, that flour came from a mill in Saskatoon, Regina, Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge, Humboldt, or a number of places which had mills and which supplied flour to the surrounding areas. These mills were built on the resources that were there, the resources of farm products, and the production of wheat. If you go to buy a bag of wheat in a store in Edmonton, Mr. Speaker, the chances are that that bag of wheat will not have been ground in western Canada but in Sarnia or even in London, Ontario. The basis for using the present resources of western Canada for diversification needs more than just the idea that they will do it. There needs to be more support than that.
I do not want to contradict this particular kind of diversification. I am trying to put forward the fact that if resource development is the method to be used, then it will take a different kind of structure from what has been used in the past. This Bill does not do that.
There is another factor about this idea of building on the resources that are there which needs to be mentioned. It implies that those resources are evenly spread across the West, that there are resources in every area that can be developed so that that particular region or subregion of the West can develop without any problem. That is not at all true as you know, Mr. Speaker, since you come from the West.
There are some regions which are obviously more poor, or very poor, with respect to any type of resource that can be developed. If one is depending upon the strength of the resources in one particular area for diversification, then that will not be possible if the area is very poor in resources anyway. The obvious strength or lack of strength as far as resources are concerned means that subregions which are obviously poor in resources are not going to develop in the same way as those that are already strong in resources.
A third point which should be put on the record as far as this new Department is concerned is that we also have a new Department of Industry, Science and Technology, which has been given much of DRIE's earlier responsibility for national regional development. This new Department was supposed to include the responsibility to reconcile the regional development policy with other industrial policies. That type of approach was
April 28, 1988

intended to reduce regional disparities. It has not effectively done that in the past when it was called DRIE, or as the Department of Industry, Science and Technology. There has really been no indication that this will happen in a new Department which would be established.
Small business people in the West have taken a good and hard look at diversification. Mr. Bulloch, for instance, has indicated that diversification needs to be overhauled, and that the whole process needs to be looked at very thoroughly. They have indicated that they do not believe that this small fledgling Department without any money will be able to do the kind of co-ordinating which is one of its responsibilities.
If we look at one initiative that this Department will take, we see that it is to co-ordinate those large Departments such as the Department of Transport, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of National Health and Welfare, and any of the other large Departments. The Government is being naive in believing that this fledgling Department can be an effective co-ordinator of these large Departments. DRIE had exactly that same co-ordinating responsibility. DRIE's capacity to coordinate the activities of federal Departments and agencies was extremely limited. It had that responsibility and it was unable to fulfil it. I take this from the report delivered by small business groups.
It was unable to do it mostly because the bureaucracy is such that it does not have enough clout to say to the Department of Transport, for example, that this is the type of action that it must take in a particular area. The Ministers of Transport, Health, and Agriculture did not welcome DRIE's attempts to promote some kind of co-ordination among them. In fact, it worked exactly the opposite in many cases. Because of these feelings of need for diversification by DREE, they felt they had to resist it.
