Mr. Speaker, I rise in the time available before Question Period to discuss the initiative to establish the western diversification office for western Canada. This initiative by the Government is not fully understood. Some discussions have gone on in committee and in previous debate in the House. I recall that the debate on second reading was a relatively short one.
This office is part of an initiative by the federal Government to establish regional offices to do very much what the old DRIE and other economic and regional development initiatives had been doing previously. To some extent it is a question of changing the names on the signs and some of the activities. Actions that were in place under the previous Government and the existing Government will continue to be worked into the mandate of the western development initiative office.
In terms of function, our understanding is that there will be a Deputy Minister located in Edmonton, with regional offices in Winnipeg, Saskatoon, and Vancouver and a liaison office in Ottawa which will be headed up by an Assistant Deputy Minister. This liaison in Ottawa is probably quite crucial to the activities. You will see why, Mr. Speaker, when we review some of the criticisms that have been levelled at the initiative by some people speaking for small business across the country. For instance, on March 18 of this year John Bulloch was quoted in the press as indicating that the $1.2 billion western diversification program is "dangerously close to becoming nothing more than a political slush fund". John Bulloch, as Hon. Members know, is the President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. He and his association took a close look at this $1.2 billion initiative which involves $1.2 billion spread over five years. The amounts of money involved are not as grand as they would first sound.
This federation represents 20,000 small business members across Canada who are concerned that the initial actions of the Government under the heading of regional and western diversification appear to be "feathering the nests of the provincial Governments and propping up the federal Government's vulnerable constituencies". The small business people were not terribly impressed by the proposal which first came out.
The federation's director for Alberta, Doug Wright, pointed to the awarding of $9.5 million for the Daishowa pulp mill which is near Peace River as being one example of what he
describes as misspending by the Edmonton Western Diversification Office. Mr. Wright said that it is difficult to believe that the Daishowa decision on this profitable investment hinged on the relatively small western diversification strategy contribution.
Indeed, I would observe that it seems rather strange that there should be western development funding for this very large initiative when the Government's indication was that it would be focusing its attention on the small and medium-sized businesses. Under almost anyone's description of what is a big and a medium-sized business, this particular one would fall into the big category.
In its initial steps at least, the Government's approach appears to be more political than economic. Structurally, the intention of the Government is to leave the impression that it is moving sources of power away from Ottawa and into Edmonton, the centre of western Canada. We are left with the impression that this will somehow improve the decisionmaking that will be made in the interests of western Canadians. That is a song we have been hearing the Government sing throughout the four years of its current mandate. Yet the results from the singing of this song make us wonder why it bothers.
In the areas in which the Government has some ability to influence and interfere within its own Departments, we see that it has done a very poor job of representing western Canada. In the fiscal year 1984-85, the year the Government took power, the four western provinces received as a percentage of national government purchases 13.9 per cent of the business. That was not up to the standards one would expect, given the population and the economic activity generated in western Canada.
We now have the statistics for the two years following. In the first year this Government, which was supposed to be helping western Canada and encouraging business in western Canada, was in power, it dropped its purchasing from western Canada from 13.9 per cent down to 12 per cent, and the following year purchases from western Canada dropped even lower, to 11.5 per cent. Western Canadian business lost the opportunity to do business with the Government of Canada under the aegis of this Conservative Government, a Government which spoke loudly about how it would help western Canada and divert more business to that region. In fact, it ran the other way.

GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
subsubtopic: COUNTERVAIL DUTY ON EUROPEAN BEEF RULED ILLEGAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada must decide whether to accept GATT's ruling that the countervail imposed by the Canadian Import Tribunal on European beef is illegal. Our choice is to continue with the countervail or to drop the tariff in favour of a quota system.
Canada tried quotas before, way after the damage had already been done, and they did not work too well. Besides, why should cattlemen have to put up with any imports of highly subsidized hamburger meat? It is not fair to our livestock industry.
I think the international tribunal should be reminded that cattle producers should have a say in what affects their industry, even if the commodity they produce does get transformed through processing.
This was the point at issue. It needs to be reinforced. I urge the Minister to say "no" to the GATT ruling on May 30.

Mr. Speaker, one would have thought that France might have learned its lesson at Dien Bien Phu. French arms were equally ineffective in Indo-China and North Africa as the people of those regions struggled against the French colonialists.
Today we learn that France has dispatched more troops to fight the Kanaks in New Caledonia. Bloodshed will result, but in the end independence will be won.
The last vestiges of French imperialism in North America, France's hold on St. Pierre and Miquelon, and their fraudulent claim to Canadian fish stocks, are without warrant.
Imperialism in today's world is a spent force. The sooner France realizes this the better.

Mr. Speaker, since the Conservative Government came to power, subsidized housing has been shamefully neglected. First of all, the Government has done nothing for single-parent families who need subsidized housing. Second, this Government has changed the criteria, so that if you want to build cooperatives for average and low-income Canadians, the cost of participating is now $500 or $600. This will not do at all for people in Laurier and Sainte-Marie, who would need rents in the area of $300.
And Outremont!

My colleague from Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) says the same applies to the poor in the Outremont section of Montreal. What this Conservative Government has done about housing is totally unacceptable. There is no home ownership program, which means that Montreal is still a city of tenants.
Mr. Speaker, I hope an election will be called very soon so that a Liberal Government can restore fairness to this particular situation.

Mr. Speaker, most countries where people have lived under a socialist government soon realize that socialism is not the answer. For instance, after experiencing socialism for several years, France acknowledged that socialism was an obstacle to the economic and social development of a country that seeks prosperity. Russia has also admitted that free enterprise would help its economy to expand, and China has reached the same conclusion.
That is why today, I wish to pay tribute to our friends in Manitoba who have realized this and, in so doing, rejected the obsolete socialist regime of the NDP, and I want to congratulate them. I am sure they will see better days in the not too distant future.

subsubtopic: BELL ISLAND, NFLD.-LACK OF PERMANENT EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the community of Bell Island in St. John's East was at one time
April 28, 1988

the most prosperous town in Newfoundland with a population of over 12,000, and over 2,000 people working in one of the most important iron ore mines in the world. They worked hard and contributed to government revenue. All that ended in 1966 when the mine closed and all the workers lost their jobs.
After 22 years Bell Islanders are still waiting for fair treatment from government. There are about 4,800 people still on Bell Island. They suffer from primitive ferry service and lack of permanent employment. Over 60 per cent unemployment exists among those of working age. Make-work jobs and short-term employment are not enough.
Bell Island is here to stay. It is time government recognized its responsibility to Bell Island and Bell Islanders. It is not too late to put special economic development programs in place. Bell Islanders want to work in dignity. Bell Island deserves more than it has received from this Government and from the last.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-REDUCTION IN AUTOMOBILE NITROGEN OXIDE EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) noted in the House on Monday and in the United States Congress yesterday, acid rain does not discriminate. Indeed, it falls on the just and unjust alike on both sides of the border. Clearly it is in our mutual best interest that Canada and the United States tackle the acid rain problem with a concerted and effective plan of action.
It is equally clear that Canada has been doing its part. For example, allowable nitrogen oxide emissions from light cars and trucks and heavy duty vehicles have been cut by 60 per cent and 50 per cent respectively. This control program is the toughest in the world.
We need take no lessons from the Liberal Party which, while in government, sat on its hands on the acid rain issue. Indeed, without question, no other Canadian Government-and certainly no other Canadian Prime Minister-has been as persistent, forthright, and substantive as our present Prime Minister in pressing the case on acid rain.
The message is getting through. The United States is being convicted by its own inaction. To quote the Chairman of its Environment Committee, Congressman Scheuer: "We ought to be embarrassed to look (Canada) in the face." The United States is well aware that the present situation is simply unacceptable.
Let me commend the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) for their actions to date, and encourage them to continue in their efforts to reclaim and protect Canada's irreplaceable natural heritage.

subtopic: S. O. 21 FINANCE TAX TREATMENT OF ARTISTS
S. O. 21 FINANCE TAX TREATMENT OF ARTISTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Committee on Communications and Culture tabled a report recommending changes to our tax system that would make it better reflect the importance of artists in strengthening our unique Canadian culture. However, the Government alone has the power to make these changes and it cannot hide behind the deficit battle on this one. We were very careful that our recommendations would not make unreasonable demands on the Treasury.
While our report was unanimous, I must speak up for the many artists who have not been helped by the Government's Budgets, who have been hurt by tax reform, and who face an uncertain future with free trade. The Government has not done enough to address the unique economic circumstances in which artists often have to live.
Our artists are an important national treasure. They do not only contribute to our culture, they are part of our culture. A nation as rich as ours can surely afford an investment in our artists. Better yet, can we afford not to?
We can be proud that we have established the importance of enhancing our unique Canadian culture. Now we must change our income tax system to help the artists who helped us build our culture. To make this happen I hope that the committee's report goes onto the Government's agenda and not onto the shelf.

subsubtopic: UNVEILING OF PLAQUE COMMEMORATING WORKERS KILLED OR INJURED ON THE JOB
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every year over 1,000 Canadians are killed on the job. Over six times that number lose their lives to cancer, lung disease, and other ailments caused by exposure to toxic substances in the workplace.
In Thunder Bay this evening, representatives from labour and the Church will join with local representatives to unveil a plaque commemorating workers who have been killed, injured, or disabled on the job.
I join these and countless other Canadians across the country on this day of mourning in calling upon all levels of government to examine and improve legislation governing occupational health and safety.
Workplace death, disability, and injury represent a national tragedy, a tragedy which hits hundreds of thousands of Canadian workers and their families every single year.
I join with the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) and our grieving and concerned labour constituents in demanding action that will save lives and prevent injuries.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF MANITOBA EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES
IMPORTANCE OF MANITOBA EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) visit to Washington has been a great success. President Reagan has reconfirmed his support for the free trade agreement between the U.S. and Canada. That is a success.
The importance of free trade to Manitoba and all western Canada cannot be overstated. Our largest industries, including agriculture, energy, aerospace, mining, forestry, and manufacturing, are directly dependent upon export sales to the United States.
Of the $1.4 billion in exports by Manitoba to the United States in 1986, 7.8 per cent was in electricity, 6.3 per cent in aircraft parts, 6.1 per cent in softwood lumber, and 4.8 per cent in motor vehicle parts.
However, the lion's share of exports to the United States from Manitoba comes from our agricultural area, with some $973 million in export sales to the United States.
Rural Manitoba's economy is dependent on and growing with the benefits of free trade. When the rural communities benefit, so does Winnipeg.
It is obvious that Manitoba and western Canada need secure access to the United States market to prosper.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-POLLUTION CONTROLS URGED FOR UNITED STATES POWER PLANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to Energy Probe in Toronto, the United States could cut its acid rain pollution of Canada in half by spending about $5 billion on pollution controls for midwestern power plants.
Energy Probe concludes that the United States could cut acidic pollution at specific U.S. power plants for far less money than a nation-wide program would cost. Energy Probe urges the Government of Canada to change its failed strategy of quiet diplomacy on acid rain against the U.S. administration.
Philip Jessup, Director of Air Quality Research for the Toronto based organization, said: "Our Government has been barking up the wrong tree by insisting that the U.S. draft a new acid rain law".
He concluded by saying: "For a total of $5 to $6 billion, the United States could cut acidic emissions in the Midwest by 50 per cent".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today before the House we are discussing the subject of western diversification. Already some 300 projects have been approved under this program, including some in my own constituency.
Air Services Consultants will receive $35,500 to complete the development of a unique disposable packaging container for transporting dangerous and infectious diagnostic specimens. Omara Systems will receive $126,500 in funds for the development of a state of the art monitoring thermostat and heat tracing controller. Ambucraft Services Ltd. will receive $48,090 to design and develop a new wheelchair lift for vans and buses.
April 28, 1988

I call upon all Members of the House to move this Bill through the House quickly and to give the western diversification initiative the additional mandate and resources that the Bill will provide.

subsubtopic: AUDITOR TRAINING ASSISTANCE TO THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of a number of Members of the House who has lived and worked in a developing country for several years, I want to make some comments about Canada's role in development. While the Government could do more in this field, there are a number of development assistance areas that are particularly important. One of these involves development of government infrastructure, specifically government auditing.
For decades, successive federal Governments and Auditors General have been active in this field. The Auditor General and his office work very closely with CIDA, the United Nations, and other international agencies in providing invaluable auditor training assistance and audit systems development aid to the Third World. Because Canada has been a pioneer in comprehensive and legislative auditing, it is only natural that we share our expertise in this field.
I want to commend the Auditor General's office for their efforts in this area and encourage them to continue this fine tradition.

speechtext:

Privilege-Mr. E. Epp
ethnocultural groups and multicultural organizations in response to the report of the committee.
This morning in the legislative committee which is dealing with the multiculturalism Bill a very similar matter arose. I will not read Citation 16 of Beauchesne's again but only emphasize that Members of Parliament who have responsibilities to deal with matters of public policy need to be aware of what the Canadian people think about these matters. They should have the opportunity to hear from multicultural organizations on their views of the matter.
Three government Members proposed a motion this morning to bring an end to consideration by the committee of testimony by witnesses on Bill C-93. The Canadian Ethnocultural Council is the only non-governmental organization which has been heard to this point. The Canadian Ethnocultural Council has proposed a number of witnesses from organizations.
A motion proposed and carried by the government majority on the committee imposed a guillotine, a six or eight-hour marathon session in which selected witnesses will be heard. Submissions from five of these six organizations will be denied.
I submit that this is a prima facie case of denial of my privileges as a Member and the critic for multiculturalism in the legislative committee. If you agree with me, Mr. Speaker, and find that, I will, of course, be very happy to move the necessary motion.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ADJUSTMENT MEASURE POLICY ON VETERANS DESIGNATED AWOL
VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ADJUSTMENT MEASURE POLICY ON VETERANS DESIGNATED AWOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have an opportunity to expand on one of the questions I raised in the House earlier this week regarding the situation of the late Mr. Gordon Broad. In 1943 at age 18 this individual joined the Canadian Army. He served in Europe until peace was declared. Since I happened to know this individual personally and knew him for many years, I am fully aware of his war record. Mr. Broad served gallantly. He, along with his comrades, were prepared to lay down their lives so that those of us today are able to live and cherish the peace and freedom that we have come to know in our country and in our part of the world.
After peace was declared in Europe, Mr. Broad volunteered for the Pacific theatre and got 30 days leave before he was about to debark. At that time in 1945, war with Japan ended. He was then age 20. He asked for industrial leave in Nanaimo, B.C. His sergeant denied the request, although Mr. Broad had a job to go to in the interior of the province. The sergeant said that men were needed to police the grounds, but for the individual troops this meant that they would be hanging around to do KP duty while awaiting their appropriate papers. Since Mr. Broad had a job to go to-he was anxious to seek employment-he left on October 17, 1945. Some of his friends and colleagues at the time were applying for and receiving leave.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that amnesty was declared for 14,000 absentees or deserters, as they were called, although in no way would these individuals be considered deserters. They had served their country well, gallantly and had been prepared to give their lives. When the war ended and peace was declared, the young men saw no reason to remain. They were
April 28, 1988

anxious to get on with their lives and with building their careers. This included Mr. Broad.
At the time amnesty was declared, Gordon Broad was prospecting in the interior of British Columbia and was unaware of it. You know from your constituency of Alberta, Mr. Speaker, that when you are in the bush prospecting you are neither listening to the news regularly nor reading daily newspapers and are, therefore, unaware of government initiatives. Such was the case here.
The 1946 Order-in-Council PC 3264 was made under the 1945 National Emergencies Transitional Powers Act. It was applicable to all service personnel who went absent on or before January 1, 1946, in Canada, and who had not been apprehended or surrendered themselves before August 15, 1946.
I received that in the letter of the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) of April 24, 1987. This Order in Council provided that such persons would be deemed never to have served in the Canadian Forces and consequently would not be entitled to any of the rights, privileges or benefits normally accorded to former members of the Armed Forces.
Mr. Broad approached the Canadian Legion a number of years ago, and through countless attempts was unsuccessful in obtaining the appropriate pardon. On August 25, 1980, a letter from the National Personnel Records Centre confirmed the Order in Council application to his record.
In early 1985, through the then Minister of National Defence, I asked that a review of Mr. Broad's case be undertaken, and the Minister of National Defence of the time wrote in a letter of June 18, 1985, that no discretionary power existed under the Order in Council for individual cases and those of the 14,000 other people affected by this, although dispensation had not been undertaken in any single case as was made clear in that letter.
On December 5, 1986, I wrote to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) asking that he review the case as Mr. Broad was not eligible for any benefits. At this time, Mr. Broad was in extremely ill health. Under doctor's orders, he had been prohibited from working. He had no income apart from his unemployment insurance benefits. I am sad to say that his wife was also ordered not to work by her physician. The Minister of Veterans Affairs sent a letter on to the Associate Minister of National Defence as he had no jurisdiction, he said, back on December 17, 1986.
The Order in Council still stands. Despite representations made on behalf of Mr. Broad and others, the Government has failed to take any action.
I wrote again to the Associate Minister of National Defence on March 10, 1987, asking if Cabinet would consider amending the Order in Council to enable Gordon Broad, after having served so well in the overseas theatre during the Second World
Adjournment Debate
War, to be eligible for appropriate benefits that ought to be available to veterans and particularly those who actually served overseas. On April 24, 1987, the Associate Minister of National Defence wrote that the whole question of dealing with absentees received the most careful and exhaustive examination, and in the end, it was concluded that the course of action which was followed was the best and most practical way of dealing with a difficult problem. This brings little comfort to people like Mr. Broad.
The Canadian Legion made representations as early as 1946 and again over the years, but there was no alteration to the Government's position regarding that Order in Council. Today, I simply want to make an appeal on behalf of an individual who served his country throughout his entire life. He has a long record of serving his community and his country in so many different ways. It would take literally pages to list the different ways Mr. Broad and his wife have served our country.
While in this case I am referring to a specific individual, the same thing applies to many, many others. I simply want to say that I think it is appropriate now that the Government take whatever steps necessary and whatever extraordinary steps necessary to ensure that these men and women receive a pardon and that their families be eligible for the appropriate benefits that any veteran who served his or her country in the last war is eligible to receive. I am really asking the Government to give special consideration to this and to related cases.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Hawkes (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR ADJUSTMENT MEASURE POLICY ON VETERANS DESIGNATED AWOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Kamloops-Shuswap has a particular case in mind and is really asking the current Ministry to revisit history and perhaps to change it.
The Hon. Member does know that under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act of 1945, an Order in Council was passed which indicated that any Armed Forces personnel who had gone absent from Canadian Forces on or before January 1, 1946, in Canada, and who had not been apprehended or had not surrendered themselves before August 15, 1946, close to some eight months later, would be deemed never to have served in the Canadian Forces.
That was the decision made at the time to accomplish two things, to be fair to those who had served with distinction and had obeyed the rules in the situation in force at that time, and to recognize that some people leaving the Forces without the proper papers of discharge were doing so for some perceived actual or real advantage to themselves by not doing what was required of them at that time.
That would have created quite a large problem because there were about 14,000 absentees or deserters who fell into that category. Somehow their lives needed to be regulated. They needed to be able to return to civilian life and not have their futures destroyed. That was the decision taken by the

April 28, 1988
Adjournment Debate
politicians of the time. That is why the Order in Council was passed and it did indeed accomplish that.
Very strong representations were made on this issue in 1972. The issue was reconsidered and the decision was made that the original Order in Council should stand and should be upheld for the reasons which I have outlined.
The matter can be reviewed in an individual case if there is something on the file which indicates that a mistake was made. In the 40 years during which this order has been in existence, individual petitions have been made and files have been examined but no such mistake has been uncovered.
In response to the Hon. Member's question on April 26 the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) told him, and repeats today, that it is the Government's decision to abide by the Order in Council of 1946. It was fair and just and remains so.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HONEY PRODUCERS BE GIVEN GOVERNMENT COMPENSATION
REQUEST THAT HONEY PRODUCERS BE GIVEN GOVERNMENT COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 19 I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) which was responded to by his Parliamentary Secretary. I asked the Government what it was going to do with regard to the tremendous crisis facing honey producers in western Canada.
On January 1 the Government closed the border to bees being brought into Canada because of a parasitic varroa mite which is affecting a number of states in the United States. This is having a devastating impact on some 2,000 honey producers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, including the Peace River country.
The Government assured these producers last July that they would be able to bring in replacement bees as they do every year for their hives in western Canada. However, on January 1 the border was closed. The cost of replacement bees from other countries such as Australia and New Zealand is almost double.
I asked the Parliamentary Secretary if the Government would be prepared to provide the extra transportation costs which amount to approximately $25 per hive. I got a zero answer, a comment about the Government providing assistance under the Special Grains Program for honey producers which, of course, has nothing to do with the varroa mite problem.
That compensation is being provided because the U.S. Farm Bill has effectively dropped the price of honey in this country from at least 60 cents a pound to some 30 to 40 cents a pound. The compensation being provided under the Special Grains Program covers that, but that is another problem.
The Parliamentary Secretary tried to smother this parasite infestation problem with another problem of the United States Farm Bill driving down the price of honey and effectively gave me no answer. Time has passed and the Government has not provided the compensation. Alberta has provided some but
Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia have provided none.
The time has almost passed for transporting in replacement supplies of packaged bees from Australia or New Zealand. The Government has procrastinated for so long that we are now getting to the stage of compensation because the producers are effectively put out of business for an entire year. This will cost them tens of thousands of dollars.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will not prolong the agony these producers are facing and will announce a compensation program of at least $30 per hive, which is judged by many producers in the West as being more adequate compensation. It will allow them to get back into business in the coming year even though their income will be effectively destroyed for this year.
The Government has a responsibility to take some action in this regard. I hope it will make an announcement this afternoon for the benefit of these producers in western Canada. While it seems like a relatively small industry to those of us who are not directly involved, it does involve 2,500 jobs in western Canada and $10 million worth of honey. It impacts on millions of dollars in production of clover, seed, Canola and alfalfa because the seeds need to be properly pollinated. The industry has a broad impact across western Canada and compensation by the Government is definitely in order. It should be paid immediately.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Shirley Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subtopic: REQUEST THAT HONEY PRODUCERS BE GIVEN GOVERNMENT COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the honey industry is divided on the issue of the ban on importation of honey bees from the United States and has been for some time. Its national body, the Canadian Honey Council, has not taken a consensus position to provide advice to the Government. Instead, this issue has rested on provincial beekeepers' associations of which all but one have indicated that they are not willing to live with the risk of importing bees from the United States.
The polarization of the industry on this issue has been emphasized by the strong lobby of the beekeepers who want to import bees from the United States, and, recently, some beekeepers formed an organization called Alberta Beekeepers for Mite-Free Bees to represent the producers who favour the border closure.
Recognizing that some citizens were not well informed about the prevailing situation and to clarify facts and distribute uniform information across the country, an industry-Government meeting was held on March 23, 1988. At that time, U.S. officials in attendance outlined the progress the scientists and regulatory officers had achieved in attempting to control the varroa disease and its spread. Agriculture Canada officials are still concerned about the completeness of the scientific data and the effectiveness of regulatory measures used to assist in disease reduction in the United States. To
April 28, 1988

date, there is no indication that these will ensure 100 per cent control over the disease.
There are presently 19,000 beekeepers in Canada, of which approximately 2,000 are commercial. Together, they operate 700,000 beehives or colonies. There is a maximum of 120 commercial beekeepers who will be affected by the border closing measures, representing approximately 100,000 colonies. Of these 120 beekeepers, most are bulk honey producers and will hire about 500 people as seasonal help. At an average of 150 pounds of honey per hive, 15 million pounds of honey will be lost to production in 1988. The five-year Canadian average production is 85 million pounds. Therefore, the decrease in production is estimated at 18 per cent for an approximate value of $7 million at the current price of honey.
It is not clear how the decreased honeybee population will affect the pollination of clover and canola. While honeybees are the recommended pollinators of clovers, wild bees and leaf cutting bees also contribute to their pollination. The biology of the Canola plant also allows the plant to be productive without the presence of honeybees. This data has not been clearly researched and it would be presumptuous to attribute a dollar value to the impact of the losses of honeybees to these crops.
Alternative sources of bees have been available to supply the increased Canadian demand. Agriculture Canada officials, as well as provincial Government officials and some beekeepers, have been in close contact with New Zealand and Australia who awaited bee orders to gear up production all winter. We are familiar with the Australian animal health system and have confidence in its regulatory measures. There is no evidence that varroa and tracheal mites exist in that country and we have concluded that bees could be safely imported from both Australia and New Zealand.
Adjournment Debate
Canadian beekeepers were also willing to provide bees to their fellow package bee operators. The problem, therefore, was not one of supply, but of price. The Special Canadian Grains Program should help to ease part of the financial crisis faced by beekeepers. The Province of Alberta has offered financial assistance to all beekeepers to compensate the increased cost of honey production. Unfortunately, other prairie provinces have not accepted this responsibility, thus creating disparities between provinces.
We have concluded that a fair and equitable compensation payment cannot be made at this time. Eastern beekeepers did not receive compensation when the border east of Manitoba was closed in 1986. It must be pointed out that the Government has never compensated for actions to prevent the introduction of undesirable diseases into the country. As I have already mentioned, some relief will be forthcoming from the Special Canadian Grains Program and should help to alleviate the financial burden facing many honey producers. A meeting on tripartite stabilization was held at the beginning of the month. If provinces and beekeepers agree on the program, there is a strong possibility it could be in place for the 1988 marketing season.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, positive actions have been triggered by the setbacks the industry faces and I assure you that the Government will continue to work with the industry to build a strong sector.
